investigacion.base:
I couldn't open the PLATracker spreadsheet or the MND page directly, so the figures below come from news coverage and Taiwan Security Monitor (TSM) summaries of MND data. **Nothing has resolved yet; November hasn't started.** Your answer will mostly depend on whether a big named exercise happens in November. Without one, 2026's pattern points to a daily maximum of roughly 15–30, set by a routine "joint combat readiness patrol" (JCRP). With one, it could be 70–130 or more.

**Check before forecasting: which number does the resolution column use?** Sources report two figures: all aircraft detected around Taiwan, and the smaller number that actually entered the ADIZ. You should confirm in the spreadsheet which one "Total Aircraft Tracked in ADIZ" holds, because the difference is often 20–40%. For example, on Aug 4, 2026, 21 aircraft were detected but only 17 entered the ADIZ.

**Most recent news (October 2026)**
- **Oct 5–11:** MND counted 56 PLA aircraft over the week's seven activity days, up 21.7 percent from 46 the week before, and 34 aircraft entered Taiwan's ADIZ. No aircraft were detected on October 3, 4 and 5, while the patrols produced 14 aircraft on October 6 and 21 on October 9.
- **Pace of patrols:** the Oct 6 and Oct 9 patrols plus one on Sept 30 made three in 11 days. China has issued no-sail notices for live-fire drills from October 12 to 17.
- **Oct 17:** 9 aircraft detected, "5 out of 9 sorties crossed the median line and entered Taiwan's northern, central and southwestern part ADIZ".
- **Oct 18:** 2 aircraft, both of which entered the ADIZ.

**Base rates for 2026: much lower than 2025**
- **Overall level:** ADIZ entries between January 1 and August 9 were 1,200 PLA aircraft, against 2,501 over the same window of 2025 — a 52 percent drop. Monthly ADIZ totals in 2026 have run between 121 and 216 aircraft; in 2025 the range was 222 to 392.
- **Monthly single-day peaks (all aircraft detected, not just ADIZ entries):**
  - January: the Jan 15 patrol, with 34 aircraft, was the highest single-day total.
  - March 17: the last day with more than 30 aircraft, as of early June.
  - May: peaked at 29 aircraft on both May 1 and May 25.
  - August: 21 aircraft on August 4 (17 ADIZ entries) and 11 on August 15 (7 ADIZ entries), plus 20 aircraft with 15 ADIZ entries on Aug 18.
  - October so far: 21 on Oct 9.
- **Quiet spells:** there have been long pauses, such as seven consecutive days, from February 27 to March 5, 2026, on which not a single PLA aircraft was reported inside the zone. Activity also stopped entirely during the Trump–Xi summit on May 14–15.
- **Large exercises:** the record is 111 aircraft inside the ADIZ on October 14, 2024, during the Joint Sword-2024B exercise. On Dec 29, 2025, Justice Mission-2025 put about 130 aircraft around Taiwan. Before that, the high marks were 71 on Dec 26, 2022, and 49 on Aug 5, 2022, after Pelosi's visit.
- **Typical 2026 month:** JCRPs happen roughly 2–4 times a month, and each one usually sets that month's peak at about 15–34 aircraft.

**Things to watch before and during November**
- Whether the October live-fire notices (Oct 12–17) grow into a named exercise. If one happens, it could also be repeated in November.
- Any US arms sales, transits by Lai Ching-te, or high-level US–China meetings in November. Large exercises have usually followed political triggers, while summits have brought pauses.
- The Spring Festival lull doesn't apply to November.

**Current status:** nothing has resolved. If 2026's pattern holds, the likeliest outcome is a peak of about 15–25 ADIZ entries, or 20–30 if the column counts all aircraft detected. There is a fat upper tail if a named exercise takes place. I didn't find any prediction-market prices for this question.

criterios: This question will resolve as the maximum number of aircraft that Taiwan reports having violated its air defense identification zone (ADIZ) in a single day during November 2026. Resolution will be determined according to the [PLATracker's](https://www.platracker.com/trackers) spreadsheet, T[aiwan ADIZ Violations](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1qbfYF0VgDBJoFZN5elpZwNTiKZ4nvCUcs5a7oYwm52g).

If the tracker has not been updated to include data through November 2026, Metaculus will fill in any missing information using the [reports published by Taiwan's Ministry of National Defense](https://www.mnd.gov.tw/PublishTable.aspx?Types=%E5%8D%B3%E6%99%82%E8%BB%8D%E4%BA%8B%E5%8B%95%E6%85%8B&title=%E5%9C%8B%E9%98%B2%E6%B6%88%E6%81%AF) (MND), following the same date convention and methodology as the spreadsheet.

(a) **Time left:** November 1–30, 2026 is about 2–6 weeks away. The outcome will be known in early December 2026, once PLATracker and Taiwan's MND have posted their data.

(b) **If nothing changed:** 2026 has run at about half of 2025's activity. Monthly peaks come from routine "joint combat readiness patrols" and run about 15–25 aircraft entering the ADIZ, or 20–34 counting all aircraft detected. I expect the spreadsheet column "Total Aircraft Tracked in ADIZ" counts ADIZ entries, but I couldn't confirm this, which is a source of uncertainty. A typical peak would be about 18–22.

(c) **If the current trend continued:** October's patrol pace (three in 11 days, with Oct 9 at 21 aircraft) points to a November peak of roughly 17–25.

(d) **Experts and markets:** There are no prediction-market prices. Analyst summaries describe low-level but unpredictable pressure. Large named exercises have followed political triggers. Several November events could push either way:
- the APEC leaders' meeting in Shenzhen, which could bring restraint around summit diplomacy;
- Taiwan's local elections on Nov 28, which could bring pressure or restraint;
- any US arms sales.

(e) **Low scenario:** US–China diplomacy around APEC, plus restraint before Taiwan's election, produces a long lull. Patrols are small and the peak is only about 8–12 aircraft.

(f) **High scenario:** A US arms package, a statement by Lai Ching-te or an election-related trigger prompts a named exercise like Justice Mission-2025 or Joint Sword-2024B. The peak would then be 70–130+. I put the chance at roughly 5–8%. A smaller surge of 35–45 is somewhat more likely.

(a) **The time left until the outcome to the question is known:** 
The month of November 2026 begins in 13 days and concludes on November 30, 2026, meaning the outcome will be fully known in approximately 43 days (around December 1, 2026).

(b) **The outcome if nothing changed:** 
Under current baseline operational rhythms observed in 2026, the PLA conducts 2 to 4 Joint Combat Readiness Patrols (JCRPs) per month without staging massive named exercises. A routine monthly peak in 2026 typically yields 18 to 24 aircraft tracked entering the ADIZ on its busiest day.

(c) **The outcome if the current trend continued:** 
Overall PLA air activity around Taiwan in 2026 has been running roughly 50% lower than in 2025. Peak single-day detections in recent months have mostly capped out around 20–25 aircraft detected (translating to roughly 15–20 entering the ADIZ). Continuing this subdued operational profile would produce a November peak around 18–22 ADIZ violations.

(d) **The expectations of experts and markets:** 
Analysts observe that absent major geopolitical catalysts (e.g., high-level US congressional visits, significant arms package announcements, or political declarations), monthly peaks are governed by standard JCRPs (15–30 ADIZ entries). However, military monitors retain awareness of fat-tail risks where punitive drills (such as Joint Sword iterations) can rapidly push single-day ADIZ entry figures to between 70 and 110+.

(e) **An unexpected scenario that results in a low outcome:** 
Severe adverse weather throughout the Taiwan Strait (such as unseasonal late-year typhoons or prolonged winter storm fronts), coupled with bilateral diplomatic detente or summitry following the US midterm elections, results in minimal PLA sorties, leaving the month's highest single-day count at fewer than 10 ADIZ violations.

(f) **An unexpected scenario that results in a high outcome:** 
A perceived diplomatic or sovereignty provocation—such as a major US political delegation visit post-election, transit diplomacy, or advanced weapons delivery—prompts the PLA to launch a large-scale named blockade exercise (e.g., Joint Sword-2026 or a Justice Mission-style drill), driving single-day ADIZ incursions past 70 to 100+ sorties.
